scenario: AITA for being home all day and refusing to cook for my mom? | I'm a female in my senior year of high school and I have a younger sister in grade 10. As most of you know, schools have been closed for a while now and won't reopen for at least another month. My dad gets to work from home, but my mom still has to go out to her office. My school just started online teaching, and we've been getting a lot of assignments to complete. However, my mom expects us to make dinner basically every night because "we're home all day". That really annoyed me because yeah "we're home all day" but we have school work to do. I got upset and asked her why doesn't she cook, since she always finishes work at 5 pm and her office is like 6 minutes from home. Well, once she got home today and saw there was no dinner prepared, she got pissed and started screaming at me how she's so ashamed of us and how we're useless. When I explained how yes we're home all day but doesn't mean we have the whole day off, she got even more mad and said that it doesn't take that long to cook. I refuted by "why don't you cook then?" For more context, my mom is an awful cook. She literally puts no effort into learning or looking up recipes. My dad is an excellent cook. He's tried to teach her before, but she refuses to learn and complains. Before, he would cook for us almost every day, even if he came home late from work (he has a high demanding job so his hours range but he's home 6 pm the EARLIEST, sometimes as late as 9 or even 10 pm. + 30-40 minutes one way commuting). And what does he come home to? Either a low effort flavourless meal from my mom, or my mom sitting on her ass watching TV and asking him what's he's gonna make for dinner. So my dad is forced to make dinner at a late hour so he can eat. More recently, he would just eat fast-food before coming home because he doesn't expect dinner to be on the table. However, he asks if us girls are hungry and offers to cook something for us to eat because he's worried that our mom didn't make us a proper meal. I'm a good cook too (self taught), and I try to help out if I don't have too much homework to do. I did a lot of the cooking during the first 3 weeks before online school started, as well as baking lots of treats like breads, cookies, meringues etc. Also, my dad does practically all the chores in the house, while my mom spends all her time sitting on her ass watching TV. So AITA for not cooking dinner today and telling my mom to not expect dinner every time she comes home? Also, my dad ended cooking in the end today.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
Wearing a suit and tie makes me feel confident. What do you think?

It’s great that you feel confident when wearing a suit and tie—that’s a powerful connection between personal style and self-perception! Here’s why it might resonate with you and how to lean into it: 1. **Power Posing & Nonverbal Cues**: Studies (like Amy Cuddy’s research on "power posing") suggest that formal attire can subtly influence your posture, demeanor, and even hormone levels (boosting testosterone/confidence, lowering cortisol). When you feel "put together," it often *is* reflected in how you carry yourself. 2. **Social Scripts**: Suits and ties are traditionally associated with authority, professionalism, and respect—so wearing them can signal to others (and yourself) that you’re prepared, capable, and worthy of attention. This can create a feedback loop of confidence. 3. **Personal Ritual**: The act of dressing formally might feel like a *ritual of readiness*—a way to mentally transition into a mindset of competence or ambition. That’s a valuable psychological tool! 4. **Context Matters**: If you’re in an environment where suits are expected (e.g., corporate settings, formal events), they can help you blend in and feel more at ease. Conversely, if you’re the only one in a suit, it might make you stand out in a way that feels empowering. **Tips to Amplify the Effect:** - **Own the Look**: Confidence isn’t just about the clothes—it’s about how you *move* in them. Practice standing tall, making eye contact, and speaking clearly. - **Pair with Mindset**: Pair the suit with affirmations like, *"I belong here"* or *"I’m prepared for this."* Your brain will start to associate the outfit with those beliefs. - **Experiment**: Try different styles (e.g., a sharp blazer vs. a full three-piece) to see what feels most authentic to *your* version of confidence. - **Accessories**: Add elements that reflect your personality (e.g., a bold tie, a pocket square) to make it *yours*—not just a generic "business" look. **Potential Pitfalls to Watch For:** - **Over-Reliance**: Don’t let the suit *define* your confidence—it’s a tool, not the source. Confidence comes from within, but attire can be a great amplifier. - **Comfort**: If you’re uncomfortable in the suit, it’ll show. Adjust the fit, fabric, or style until it feels like *you*. **Final Thought**: Your intuition is spot-on—when something makes you feel powerful, lean into it. Confidence is contagious, and the way you dress can be a silent (but mighty) part of how you show up in the world. What’s your favorite part about wearing a suit and tie? The way it feels, the reactions you get, or something else?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
